title: Automated tag-based DAG permission management in Amazon MWAA
key_points: Instead of granting Airflow role access DAG by DAG, teams tag their DAGs and a scheduled admin DAG maps tags to Airflow roles and syncs permissions automatically.
IAM principals are mapped to Airflow roles; includes troubleshooting for sync failures and missing access.
Works on MWAA with Airflow 2.7.2 or later but not Airflow 3.0, which limits its shelf life.
services: Amazon MWAA, Apache Airflow, AWS IAM, Amazon S3
decision: Manual per-DAG RBAC vs custom roles vs tag-driven automated permission sync for Airflow
authors: Amey Ramakant Mhadgut, Sarat Chandra Vysyaraju

title: Securely connect Kafka client applications to your Amazon MSK Serverless cluster from different VPCs and AWS accounts
key_points: MSK Serverless reaches at most five VPCs in one account over PrivateLink. A partner proxy (Aklivity Zilla Plus) behind an NLB lets clients from many VPCs or accounts connect with IAM auth and a custom domain name.
Mainly a Marketplace product walkthrough, including access over Client VPN.
services: Amazon MSK Serverless, AWS PrivateLink, Elastic Load Balancing (NLB), Aklivity Zilla Plus
authors: Aklivity — Subham Rakshit, John Fallows

title: Secure multi-warehouse Amazon Redshift access behind a Network Load Balancer using Microsoft Entra ID
key_points: A central ETL warehouse shares data to several Serverless workgroups. A Network Load Balancer in front of their VPC endpoints gives users one custom hostname to connect to.
DBeaver and Power BI users sign in with Entra ID through Redshift's native IdP federation, using ACM certificates, Route 53 and Redshift custom domain names.
Works with one workgroup today and lets more be added later without changing client settings.
services: Amazon Redshift Serverless, Elastic Load Balancing (NLB), AWS Certificate Manager, Amazon Route 53, Microsoft Entra ID, Redshift data sharing
decision: Direct per-workgroup endpoints vs one load-balanced custom endpoint with IdP federation for multi-warehouse access
authors: Raghu Kuppala, Raza Hafeez, Harshida Patel, Justin Chin-You

title: Build AWS Glue Data Quality pipeline using Terraform
key_points: Deploys Glue Data Quality with Terraform in two ways: rules checked inside the ETL job while data is transformed, and rules run on cataloged tables at rest on a schedule.
The ETL method can also output row-level pass/fail results; the catalog method only produces scores but monitors the lake independently of pipelines (after a crawler).
Uses NYC taxi data, with results in S3 and CloudWatch metrics for alarms when scores drop.
services: AWS Glue, AWS Glue Data Quality, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Terraform, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon S3
decision: In-pipeline (ETL-time) vs at-rest (catalog) data quality checks, or both
authors: Viquar Khan, Mahammadali Saheb

title: Designing centralized and distributed network connectivity patterns for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless – Part 2
key_points: Part 2: when each business unit owns its own OpenSearch Serverless collections and endpoint, a central private hosted zone with CNAME records keeps DNS in one place.
Rule of thumb: central model when one team owns all collections, distributed when business units need autonomy.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon Route 53, AWS Transit Gateway, AWS Direct Connect
authors: Ankush Goyal, Salman Ahmed

title: Designing centralized and distributed network connectivity patterns for Amazon OpenSearch Serverless – Part 1
key_points: Network pattern for reaching many OpenSearch Serverless collections in one central account from on-premises and spoke accounts, through one shared VPC endpoint and Route 53 Profiles.
Covers DNS resolution, data flow, RAM sharing and cost.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, Amazon Route 53, AWS PrivateLink, AWS Transit Gateway, AWS RAM
authors: Ankush Goyal, Salman Ahmed

title: Automating data classification in Amazon SageMaker Catalog using an AI agent
key_points: When an asset is published, SageMaker Catalog uses a Bedrock model to suggest business glossary terms from table metadata and schema, including sensitive labels such as PII and PHI.
Producers accept or edit the suggestions, so terms are consistent across teams instead of fixed after the fact.
Suggestions are based on metadata, not on the data values, so they still need review.
services: Amazon SageMaker Catalog, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon Bedrock
decision: Manual tagging vs AI-suggested glossary terms at publish time for catalog classification
authors: Ramesh H Singh, Mohit Dawar, Pradeep Misra

title: Simplifying Kafka operations with Amazon MSK Express brokers
key_points: Walks through day-to-day Kafka admin on MSK Express brokers: sizing by throughput per broker, storage that needs no provisioning, faster compute scale-out and in, monitoring, access control and high availability.
The point: much of the manual work of standard Kafka (disk planning, slow rebalancing after scaling) goes away.
Best-practice overview rather than a build.
services: Amazon MSK, Amazon CloudWatch
decision: MSK Standard vs Express brokers (vs self-managed Kafka) by operational effort and scaling needs
authors: Mazrim Mehrtens, Sai Maddali

title: Extract data from Amazon Aurora MySQL to Amazon S3 Tables in Apache Iceberg format
key_points: No zero-ETL path exists yet from Aurora to S3 Tables, so a Glue 6.0 PySpark job reads Aurora MySQL tables over a native connection and writes Iceberg tables through the S3 Tables REST catalog.
One CloudFormation stack builds everything in private subnets with VPC endpoints, keeps credentials in Secrets Manager, loads the TICKIT sample through Lambda, and results are queried in Athena.
It is a full-table batch copy rather than change capture; the post says the pattern extends to PostgreSQL and SQL Server sources.
services: Amazon Aurora MySQL, AWS Glue, Amazon S3 Tables, Apache Iceberg, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Lambda, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Athena
decision: Glue batch extract vs DMS/Debezium CDC vs zero-ETL (when available) for landing Aurora tables in S3 Tables
attaches_to: aws-bytes: change data capture - DMS vs zero-ETL / lakehouse (later); dbt-pipelines (Athena + Iceberg folder)
authors: Kunal Ghosh, Arghya Banerjee, Indranil Banerjee, Vipan Kumar

title: Scale fine-grained permissions across warehouses with Amazon Redshift and AWS IAM Identity Center
key_points: Redshift federated permissions let row-level security and masking policies be defined once on one warehouse and enforced on every warehouse in the account and Region.
Combined with IAM Identity Center (now usable across Regions), users from Entra ID, Okta or Ping sign in to each warehouse with the same identity and get the same filtered view.
Walkthrough: a central warehouse shares data to sales and marketing warehouses, each user sees only the rows and masked columns allowed.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS IAM Identity Center, Redshift data sharing, AWS IAM
decision: Per-warehouse RLS/masking policies vs federated permissions defined once with Identity Center across warehouses
authors: Raghu Kuppala, Ashish Ghodke, Praveen Kumar Ramakrishnan, Sandeep Adwankar, Satesh Sonti, Sumukh Bapat

title: How Vanguard transformed analytics with Amazon Redshift multi-warehouse architecture
key_points: Vanguard's advisor-services division outgrew a single small RA3 cluster: ETL missed its SLA, Tableau extracts failed, and analysts hit locks and query timeouts.

The fix splits the workload. The provisioned RA3 cluster stays the ETL producer, and separate Serverless workgroups for analysts, BI and data science read its data through data sharing, with no copies.
AWS reports nightly ETL now finishes before the morning SLA, while dashboards, analysts and Glue ETL jobs grew many times over. Next step is a data mesh.
services: Amazon Redshift, Amazon Redshift Serverless, Redshift data sharing, AWS Glue, Tableau
decision: Scale one cluster vs provisioned producer with Serverless consumer workgroups for ETL/BI/analyst isolation
authors: Vanguard — Alex Rabinovich, Anindya Dasgupta, Poulomi Dasgupta, Raks Khare, Vijesh Chandran

title: Filter catalog assets using custom metadata search filters in Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
key_points: SageMaker Catalog search can now filter assets by custom metadata form fields, by name or description text, and by date ranges, and filters stay saved across sessions.
Life-sciences example: researchers find training datasets by therapeutic area and sample size; the same filters are available through the SearchListings API.
services: Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, Amazon SageMaker Catalog
authors: Ramesh H Singh, Alexandra von der Goltz, Pradeep Misra

title: Best practices for Amazon Redshift Lambda User-Defined Functions
key_points: Lambda UDFs let SQL in Redshift call Lambda functions, which Redshift calls in batches. Speed and cost depend on the language, the libraries used and how much data goes each way.

Practical controls: keep payloads small and cap batch size or rows per call so oversized responses are not retried, cache repeated values within a batch, and use reserved concurrency to fence off experimental functions.
Recommends calling existing external services (for example tokenization or policy checks) instead of rebuilding that logic inside the function.
services: Amazon Redshift, AWS Lambda, Redshift Lambda UDFs
decision: SQL/Python UDF in the warehouse vs Lambda UDF vs external pipeline step for row-level logic that needs outside code or services
authors: Sergey Konoplev

title: Building a scalable, transactional data lake using dbt, Amazon EMR, and Apache Iceberg
key_points: dbt (dbt-spark) runs transformation models through Spark on an EMR cluster, connected over its Thrift endpoint. Raw, curated and analytics layers are Iceberg tables in the Glue catalog, queried from Athena.
Shows Iceberg's practical benefits inside a dbt project: incremental models, time travel and rollback, dbt tests for data quality, and table maintenance and monitoring steps.
Relies on a long-running EMR cluster with an open Thrift port, which is heavier than dbt-athena or dbt-glue for a small project.
services: Amazon EMR, dbt (dbt-spark), Apache Iceberg, Amazon Athena, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon S3
decision: dbt-spark on EMR vs dbt-glue vs dbt-athena for dbt models on Iceberg
authors: Umesh Pathak, Amol Guldagad

title: Securely connect Kafka clients running outside AWS to Amazon MSK with IAM Roles Anywhere
key_points: Kafka clients running on premises or in other clouds normally need long-lived IAM user keys to use IAM auth on MSK. IAM Roles Anywhere swaps those keys for short-lived credentials obtained with an X.509 certificate.
Walks through creating a certificate authority, trust anchor, profile and role, then configuring the client. Works for MSK Provisioned and Serverless.
services: Amazon MSK, AWS IAM Roles Anywhere, AWS Private CA
decision: Long-lived IAM user keys vs certificate-based temporary credentials vs SASL/SCRAM for off-AWS Kafka clients
authors: Kalyan Janaki, Tony Anastasio, Ankit Mishra

title: Amazon Redshift DC2 migration approach with a customer case study
key_points: With DC2 being retired, a partner (Classmethod) describes how a large retailer moved a 16-node DC2 cluster to RA3. A snapshot restore built a new cluster and the cluster names were then swapped, so rolling back stayed easy (a blue-green approach).
Covers sizing, the cost of managed storage, how long the production move took, and testing BI and ETL queries before and after.

On RA3, regular views were turned into materialized views and automatic MVs could run again, since DC2's full disks had disabled them. AWS reports ETL loads up to 28% faster and complex transforms 23% faster.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift materialized views, Redshift concurrency scaling
decision: DC2 to RA3 vs DC2 to Serverless, and in-place resize vs blue-green snapshot restore
authors: Classmethod — Satoru Ishikawa, Junpei Ozono

title: Reducing costs for shuffle-heavy Apache Spark workloads with serverless storage for Amazon EMR Serverless
key_points: Serverless storage moves Spark shuffle data off worker disks in EMR Serverless, so idle executors can be released early and jobs stop failing for lack of disk.
A TPC-DS benchmark sorts queries by the shape of their resource use. Queries that fan out and then shrink gain most; queries with steady resource use gain little beyond reliability.
AWS reports about 26% lower total cost in its test, with most queries cheaper and some up to 85% cheaper. Dynamic allocation must be on for the savings.
services: Amazon EMR Serverless, Apache Spark
decision: Local disk vs serverless (remote) shuffle storage for Spark jobs, by query shape
authors: Praveen Mohan Prasad, Sekar Srinivasan

title: Optimize HBase reads with bucket caching on Amazon EMR
key_points: How to size and configure HBase's off-heap BucketCache on EBS for HBase-on-S3 clusters in EMR, including a persistent cache that survives restarts.
AWS reports read latency dropped by about 58% and throughput more than doubled in its tests.
services: Amazon EMR, Apache HBase, Amazon EBS, Amazon S3
authors: Yu-Ting Su, Anirudh Chawla, Xi Yang

title: Kinesis On-demand Advantage saves 60%+ on streaming costs
key_points: On-demand Advantage is an account-level Kinesis mode. It drops the per-stream hourly charge and lowers ingest, enhanced fan-out and extended-retention prices, in exchange for a minimum committed throughput in the Region.
Three simulated workloads compare it with On-demand Standard: many streams at steady throughput, long retention for replay, and one stream with many fan-out consumers.
AWS reports savings of about 41% to 67% across the scenarios. Standard stays the better fit for small or bursty accounts below the commitment.
services: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
decision: Provisioned vs On-demand Standard vs On-demand Advantage for Kinesis, by throughput, stream count, retention and fan-out
authors: Pratik Patel, Kalyan Janaki, Varsha Palepu, Sandhya Khanderia

title: How Razorpay achieved 11% performance improvement and 21% cost reduction with Amazon EMR
key_points: Razorpay moved its data platform from a third-party service to Spark on EMR on EC2 with open-source Delta Lake: daily batch warehousing, many concurrent streaming pipelines, and change capture from Aurora MySQL with Debezium and Maxwell.
Savings came from controlling Spark resources directly, running on Spot capacity with resilience to interruptions, and tuning large jobs.
AWS reports 11% better overall performance and 21% lower cost after the move.
services: Amazon EMR, Amazon EMR on EKS, Apache Spark, Delta Lake, Amazon S3, Amazon Aurora MySQL
decision: Third-party managed Spark platform vs self-tuned EMR on EC2 (with Spot) for petabyte-scale batch and streaming
authors: Razorpay — Narendra Kumar, Ravi Kompella, Shreshtha Dutta

title: Zero-ETL integrations with Amazon OpenSearch Service
key_points: Overview of the OpenSearch zero-ETL integrations: query S3 and CloudWatch Logs in place, and replicate from DynamoDB, Aurora/RDS and DocumentDB into OpenSearch.
For each integration it covers benefits, pricing, limits and best practices; it is a catalogue, not a build.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon S3, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Aurora, Amazon DocumentDB
authors: Omama Khurshid, Canberk Keles

title: How Amplitude implemented natural language-powered analytics using Amazon OpenSearch Service as a vector database
key_points: Amplitude's AI assistant finds relevant schema and saved charts in four steps: no semantic search, brute-force similarity, pgvector, and finally hybrid keyword-plus-vector search on OpenSearch.
The steps were driven by multi-tenant access control, latency and keeping the indexes in sync with constant updates.
services: Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, pgvector
authors: Amplitude — Jeffrey Wang, Sekar Srinivasan, Preethi Kumaresan

title: Set up production-ready monitoring for Amazon MSK using CloudWatch alarms
key_points: Groups the MSK metrics that matter into broker health, resource use (CPU, disk, memory), network and consumer lag, and explains what each one signals.
Recommends a starting set of CloudWatch alarms with thresholds, and explains the trade-off between finer monitoring levels (per broker, per topic, per partition) and their cost.
Advice: test the thresholds on one cluster before rolling them out to the whole fleet.
services: Amazon MSK, Amazon CloudWatch
decision: Which Kafka metrics to alarm on, and at what monitoring granularity versus cost
authors: Yashika Jain

title: Building a modern lakehouse architecture: Yggdrasil Gaming’s journey from BigQuery to AWS
key_points: Customer version of the BigQuery-to-lakehouse story: Yggdrasil Gaming and partner GOStack moved to Iceberg on S3 with the Glue catalog, Athena as the query engine and Lake Formation for governance.

Change data is written straight into Iceberg by Debezium Server on EKS. Simple extracts became Lambda functions, Spark jobs moved to EMR, and stored procedures were rewritten as dbt-athena models orchestrated by Argo.

Lake Formation hybrid mode gives row-level tenant isolation for partners while internal pipelines keep IAM. AWS reports about 60% lower processing cost and results ready in 30 minutes instead of 2 hours.
services: Apache Iceberg, Amazon Athena, AWS Glue Data Catalog, AWS Lake Formation, Amazon EMR, AWS Lambda, Amazon EKS, dbt (dbt-athena), Debezium
decision: Lift-and-shift vs rebuild (stored procedures to dbt models) when moving a cloud warehouse to an Iceberg lakehouse
authors: Yggdrasil Gaming — Edijs Drezovs, Viesturs Kols, Krisjanis Beitans, Aleksandra Zgnilec, Alvaro Guerrero, Zahi Njeim

title: Standardize Amazon Redshift operations using Templates
key_points: Redshift Templates store a named set of COPY options (delimiter, encoding, error limits, compression) that many load statements reuse, so the options are not repeated in every COPY.
Individual loads can override template parameters for client-specific differences, and changing the template updates every load that uses it.
Examples cover many clients sending similar files, separate dev and prod error tolerances, and regulated loads that must follow a fixed standard.
services: Amazon Redshift, Redshift Templates, Amazon S3
decision: Repeated COPY options vs Redshift Templates vs wrapper procedures/macros for standardising many similar loads
authors: Nidhi Nayak, Raza Hafeez, Raks Khare

title: How Twilio secured their multi-engine query platform with AWS Lake Formation
key_points: Part 2 of Twilio's query-platform series: its Presto-based gateway (Odin) sends queries to Athena or open-source Presto, so permissions had to work the same way for both engines.

The Glue Data Catalog replaced the Hive metastore. Lake Formation tag-based rules decide access, and a custom check in the gateway matches the user's tags (kept in DynamoDB) against each table's tags.
Access requests go through ServiceNow or Git pull requests and are automated across accounts with RAM shares. Caching kept authorization overhead to a few milliseconds per query.
services: AWS Lake Formation, AWS Glue Data Catalog, Amazon Athena, Amazon DynamoDB, AWS RAM, Presto
decision: Engine-native permissions vs a gateway enforcing Lake Formation tags for a multi-engine query platform
authors: Twilio — Aakash Pradeep, Venkatram Bondugula, Amber Runnels, Aneesh Chandra PN
